stem: analyst-ws asks a DNS server whenever it looks up a name. Which host is that DNS server? (Give its host name; the lookup tools show its address.)
explain: nslookup web-03 (or dig web-03.corp.local) names the server that answered: 10.20.0.2. A reverse lookup of that address (dig -x 10.20.0.2) gives dns-01.corp.local. Knowing which resolver a machine uses matters when DNS is filtered, logged or poisoned: whoever runs the resolver sees, and can alter, every name the machine looks up.

stem: www.corp.local is an alias, not a server of its own. Which host name does it really point to?
explain: dig www.corp.local shows a CNAME record (www.corp.local -> web-03.corp.local) followed by the A record of web-03. A CNAME is an alias: asking for the alias returns the real name and then that name's address. When a finding is reported against www, this is how you learn which machine to fix.

stem: An unknown device at 10.20.0.30 showed up in a scan. What host name does DNS give for that address (a reverse lookup)?
explain: dig -x 10.20.0.30 (or nslookup 10.20.0.30) asks for the PTR record of 30.0.20.10.in-addr.arpa and gets printer-01.corp.local. Reverse DNS turns the addresses in scan results into names, which helps decide whether a device is expected on the network. A missing PTR record (NXDOMAIN) proves nothing either way: reverse zones are often incomplete.

stem: Read the DNS answer below. What does it tell you about www.corp.local?

options.text: It is a CNAME alias of web-03.corp.local, so the address is web-03's
It is a separate server with its own address, 10.20.0.10
options.why: The address is web-03's: the CNAME line shows www points at web-03.corp.local.

options.text: The name does not exist in the zone, so the query failed
options.why: The status is NOERROR and the answer section has records; a missing name shows NXDOMAIN.

options.text: The answer came from another server's cache, not from the zone's owner
options.why: The aa flag in the header means authoritative: the server answered from its own zone.

explain: The ANSWER SECTION holds two records: a CNAME (www.corp.local to web-03.corp.local) and then the A record of web-03. The flags line shows aa (authoritative answer) and the status is NOERROR. An alias lets one server answer to several names; findings about www are findings about web-03.

stem: What address does this lookup return for web-03?

options.why: That is the DNS server that answered (the Server line), not web-03.
That is this workstation's own address.
That is the gateway, which is not the host that was looked up.

explain: The Server and Address lines at the top name the DNS server asked; the Name and Address lines below are the answer: web-03.corp.local is 10.20.0.10.

stem: In this dig output, what does the line in the ANSWER SECTION tell you?

options.text: web-03.corp.local is an alias of another host name defined in the same zone
options.why: An alias would be a CNAME record; this is an A record.

options.text: web-03.corp.local is IPv4 address 10.20.0.10, cacheable for 3600 seconds
The name does not exist, so the server returned an error status
options.why: The status is NOERROR and an answer was returned.

options.text: 10.20.0.10 is the DNS server that answered this query for us
options.why: The DNS server is shown on the SERVER line near the end.

explain: The A record maps a name to an IPv4 address. 3600 is the TTL: how long, in seconds, resolvers may cache the answer.

stem: Which line of this dig output shows the DNS server that answered?

options.text: ;; QUESTION SECTION:
options.why: That section shows what was asked, not who answered.

options.text: ;; Query time: 2 msec
options.why: That is how long the query took.

options.text: ;; flags: qr aa rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1
options.why: Those are header flags and counts for the reply.

explain: SERVER names the resolver that gave the answer and the port (53) and transport (UDP) used. It is the first place to look when an answer seems wrong.

stem: What does the +short option do for dig?

options.text: It asks the server for a shorter TTL on the answers
options.why: +short changes only how the result is printed.

options.text: It looks up only the first record of a name and stops
options.why: It prints every answer, just without the extra text.

options.text: It skips the DNS server and uses the local cache instead
options.why: The query is sent as usual; only the output is shorter.

options.text: It prints only the answers, without headers or sections

explain: dig +short is handy in scripts and quick checks. Here it shows the CNAME target and then its address.

stem: What does this TXT record publish?

options.text: An SPF policy: which addresses may send email for corp.local
The address of the mail server that accepts email for the domain
options.why: That would be an MX record, with the server's name.

options.text: The names of the name servers that are authoritative for the domain
options.why: Name servers are published in NS records.

options.text: An alias that points the domain at the web server's name
options.why: Aliases are CNAME records.

explain: SPF is published as a TXT record. v=spf1 ip4:10.20.0.0/24 -all means mail from that range is allowed and everything else should be rejected. It helps against forged senders.

stem: Which DNS record type maps a name to an IPv4 address?

options.text: AAAA
options.why: AAAA holds an IPv6 address.

options.text: A
PTR
options.why: PTR maps an address back to a name (reverse lookup).

options.text: CNAME
options.why: CNAME makes one name an alias of another.

explain: A = IPv4 address, AAAA = IPv6 address, CNAME = alias, PTR = reverse, MX = mail, NS = name servers, TXT = free text such as SPF.

stem: Which record type tells other servers where to deliver email for a domain?

options.text: TXT
options.why: TXT can carry mail policy such as SPF, but it does not say where to deliver mail.

options.text: PTR
options.why: PTR is for reverse lookups.

options.text: MX
A
options.why: A maps a name to an address; it does not mark a mail server.

explain: MX (mail exchanger) records name the servers that accept mail for the domain, with a priority.

stem: What does the answer say about 10.20.0.30?

options.text: It is an alias of web-03, the web server
options.why: The answer is a PTR record naming printer-01.corp.local; nothing mentions web-03.

options.text: It does not have a name registered in DNS
options.why: The status is NOERROR and a PTR answer is returned.

options.text: It is the DNS server that answered
options.why: The DNS server is shown on the SERVER line: 10.20.0.2.

options.text: Its name is printer-01.corp.local

explain: A reverse lookup (dig -x) asks for the PTR record of an address. Here it returns printer-01.corp.local.

stem: Why would an analyst run a reverse lookup on an unknown address found in a scan?

options.text: The name its owner gave it hints at what the device is
It shows which user is currently logged in to the device
options.why: DNS records name addresses, not users.

options.text: It lists every open port and the version of each service
options.why: That is what a port scan does.

options.text: It proves the device is safe because it has a name
options.why: A name says nothing about safety, and PTR records can be wrong.

explain: Names like printer-01 or cam-01 tell you a lot quickly. Remember it is only a hint: whoever controls the zone controls the name.

stem: The answer below shows 10.0.20.10.in-addr.arpa for the address 10.20.0.10. Why are the numbers backwards?

options.text: The address was mistyped, so dig reversed the octets while trying to correct it
options.why: The address typed was 10.20.0.10; the reversal is how reverse lookups are named.

options.text: Reverse zones list octets backwards so each network owner controls its branch
To hide the address from attackers, since reversed numbers are harder to read
options.why: It hides nothing; it is a naming rule.

options.text: The host is on the other side of the gateway, so its path runs in reverse
options.why: Location has nothing to do with it.

explain: DNS names get more specific from right to left, while IP addresses get more specific from left to right. Reversing the octets makes the network part the 'parent' name.

stem: Which record type does a reverse lookup return?

options.text: A
options.why: A records go from a name to an address, the forward direction.

options.text: CNAME
options.why: CNAME records are aliases.

options.text: PTR
TXT
options.why: TXT records carry free text.

explain: The QUESTION section shows 30.0.20.10.in-addr.arpa asked for IN PTR, and the answer is a PTR record.
